D.fit: Not here: 3-day indolent progression to coma, no seizure history

E.fit: Not here: focal spine radiation does not cause diffuse encephalopathy and coma

Immediate aggressive IV 0.9% normal saline rehydration to restore intravascular volume
Administer calcitonin for rapid calcium reduction within 4 to 6 hours
Administer IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid or pamidronate) for sustained effect
**Severe renal impairment or refractory to bisphosphonates:** denosumab (RANKL inhibitor)
**Life-threatening hypercalcemia with neurologic collapse:** emergent hemodialysis

During the past 3 days, she has been lethargic and somnolent
has not had focal neurologic signs

D.fit: Not here: elective surgery, prior competent patient refusal

Assess decision-making capacity: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, expressing choice

Determine emergency status of the planned surgical intervention

Re-evaluate patient decision-making capacity after premedication wears off

abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.name: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.scope: screening recommendations (men 65-75 who smoked), ultrasound imaging, surveillance intervals, elective repair thresholds, rupture
abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.core: Older adult with abdominal aortic dilation may remain asymptomatic until expansion or rupture; sudden abdominal/back pain and hypotension require immediate vascular rescue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking strongest modifiable risk; older age, male sex, family history, hypertension, atherosclerosis
Women have higher rupture risk at smaller diameters; most aneurysms infrarenal

rows.label: Clues
items: Incidental pulsatile expansile abdominal mass; localized persistent pain suggests symptomatic aneurysm
Rupture triad incompletely present; transient stability may reflect contained retroperitoneal hemorrhage
Blue toe/distal ischemia may result from mural thrombus embolization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Medial elastin/collagen degradation → progressive enlargement; greater wall radius increases tension
Retroperitoneal containment can briefly limit blood loss before catastrophic decompensation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** diagnoses AAA, generally diameter ≥3 cm; no contrast required
★ Stable suspected rupture or preoperative planning → **CT angiography**
Unstable suspected rupture → bedside ultrasound if immediate; no CT transport delaying surgery
Ultrasound detects aneurysm but cannot reliably exclude rupture; follow symptoms/hemodynamics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Rupture → **urgent vascular repair**, IV access, blood products; avoid delaying for complete workup
Permissive hypotension during transfer/resuscitation until hemorrhage control when clinically feasible
★ Elective repair at **≥5.5 cm men, ≥5.0 cm women**, or aneurysm-attributable symptoms
Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm/6 months → repair consideration; endovascular versus open based on anatomy/fitness
Smaller asymptomatic lesions → ultrasound surveillance below; refer vascular surgery, manage cardiovascular risks

rows.label: Complications
items: Rupture, thrombosis, distal embolization; repair → AKI, bowel ischemia, endoleak after EVAR
Aortoenteric fistula after prior graft: herald GI bleed → catastrophic hemorrhage; urgent evaluation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **one-time ultrasound men 65–75 who ever smoked**; selectively screen never-smoking men
Women never smoked/no family history → no screening; women smokers/family history → USPSTF evidence insufficient
Smoking cessation, BP control, statin for atherosclerotic disease; lifelong imaging follow-up after EVAR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; shock atypical
Aortic dissection: abrupt chest/back pain, possible pulse deficits or branch ischemia

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis; baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment injury, prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → interstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia → isotonic crystalloid; congestion → loop diuretic; avoid reflex fluids in overloaded patients
Stop culprit nephrotoxins; renal-dose drugs; AIN persisting after withdrawal → consider glucocorticoids
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

adrenal-insufficiency.name: Adrenal insufficiency
adrenal-insufficiency.scope: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), secondary adrenal insufficiency, cosyntropin stimulation test, morning serum cortisol, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement, adrenal crisis
adrenal-insufficiency.core: Weight loss, fatigue, orthostasis, and hyponatremia, or unexplained pressor-resistant shock after illness or interruption of glucocorticoids.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: autoimmune destruction, TB, bilateral hemorrhage, metastases; associated autoimmune thyroid disease
★ Secondary: **prolonged glucocorticoids**, pituitary disease/surgery/apoplexy; abrupt withdrawal risks crisis
Crisis triggers: infection, trauma, surgery, missed replacement, vomiting

rows.label: Clues
items: Anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, weakness; hypoglycemia, eosinophilia
Crisis: fever, confusion, severe volume depletion; symptoms may worsen rapidly during intercurrent illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular catecholamine response and increases ADH
Primary gland failure removes mineralocorticoids; secondary disease retains renin–angiotensin-driven aldosterone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **8 AM cortisol + ACTH**; very low cortisol supports, clearly high values argue against insufficiency
★ Equivocal basal cortisol → **cosyntropin stimulation**; inadequate assay-specific peak confirms impaired reserve
Traditional stimulated cutoff ≈18 µg/dL; newer assays may use ≈14–15; interpret laboratory standard
Primary → 21-hydroxylase antibodies, selected adrenal CT; secondary → pituitary evaluation/MRI
Recent pituitary injury may initially show normal cosyntropin response; clinical suspicion still matters

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crisis → draw blood if feasible, **IV hydrocortisone + isotonic saline**, dextrose for hypoglycemia
Do not wait for confirmatory results; treat precipitant and correct electrolytes carefully
Coexisting hypothyroidism → glucocorticoid replacement before levothyroxine to avoid decompensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated crisis → arrhythmia, circulatory collapse, death; chronic undertreatment → impaired function
Excess replacement → osteoporosis, diabetes, Cushingoid features

rows.label: Prevention
items: Stress-dose plan, emergency injectable hydrocortisone, medical alert ID; taper prolonged systemic steroids
Vomiting prevents absorption → parenteral replacement and urgent evaluation; teach sick-day plans to caregivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: SIADH: euvolemia, normal potassium and cortisol reserve
Sepsis: infection may coexist and trigger crisis
Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, cold intolerance, weight gain

table.title: Primary versus secondary
rows: Low/inappropriately normal ACTH; potassium usually normal

adrenal-insufficiency.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching; cortisol cutoffs are assay dependent.

ankle-and-foot-injuries.name: Ankle and foot injuries
ankle-and-foot-injuries.scope: Lateral ankle sprain, Ottawa ankle and foot rules, RICE therapy, functional rehabilitation, Achilles tendon rupture, plantar fasciitis, calcaneal apophysitis
ankle-and-foot-injuries.core: Mechanism, focal tenderness, weight-bearing ability, and tendon function distinguish ankle sprain from fracture and overuse foot disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Inversion while plantarflexed, prior sprain, poor balance → lateral ligament injury
Running/jumping, sudden training increase, tight calves, obesity; fluoroquinolones/steroids increase tendon rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Lateral swelling after inversion → **anterior talofibular ligament** injury most likely
Pain above ankle with external rotation/squeeze → syndesmotic sprain; recovery slower
Focal bony pain, deformity, neurovascular changes, or inability to bear weight → fracture evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament overstretch → microtears or disruption; tendon degeneration predisposes rupture
Repeated loading damages soft tissue; tendon degeneration reduces tensile strength

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ankle pain + **posterior-edge/tip malleolar tenderness** → ankle radiographs
★ Midfoot pain + **navicular or fifth-metatarsal-base tenderness** → foot radiographs
Either region: inability to take four steps immediately and during evaluation also triggers corresponding radiographs
Examine skin, pulses, sensation; persistent focal pain despite normal films → reassess occult fracture

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sprain: **protection, ice, compression, elevation**, brief analgesia; early protected weight-bearing
Functional brace + range-of-motion, strength, proprioceptive rehabilitation; avoid prolonged routine immobilization
Displaced/open fracture or neurovascular compromise → urgent orthopedics; immobilize and keep non-weight-bearing

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic instability, recurrent sprains, osteochondral talar injury
Missed syndesmotic injury → prolonged disability; immobilization → stiffness, thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Balance training and bracing** after prior sprain; gradual return when strength/function restored
Gradual training progression, supportive footwear, calf flexibility; avoid premature athletic return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lisfranc injury: plantar ecchymosis, midfoot instability; weight-bearing radiographs
Septic arthritis: fever, marked passive-motion pain; aspirate joint

table.title: Heel disorders
rows: Pop, weak plantarflexion, abnormal Thompson test
First-step morning pain; medial plantar heel
Active child; posterior heel squeeze tenderness

ankle-and-foot-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic decision rules and rehabilitation principles.

anorectal-disorders.name: Anorectal disorders
anorectal-disorders.scope: Anal fissure, internal and external hemorrhoids, anorectal abscess, fistula-in-ano, pruritus ani, topical vasodilators, fiber, sitz baths
anorectal-disorders.core: Anal pain, bleeding, swelling, or drainage requires inspection and focused examination; pain pattern distinguishes fissure, thrombosis, and infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constipation, straining, pregnancy, prolonged sitting; Crohn disease, diabetes, immunosuppression increase infection risk
Irritant soaps, moisture, fecal seepage contribute to pruritus ani

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion, fever, spreading erythema, crepitus** → evaluate necrotizing perineal infection urgently
Posterior midline fissure common; lateral/multiple fissures suggest Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy
Internal hemorrhoids lie above dentate line; prolapse may require manual reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fissure causes internal sphincter spasm and local ischemia; hemorrhoids represent enlarged vascular cushions
Cryptoglandular infection creates abscess; persistent epithelialized tract can become a fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspection first**, gentle DRE/anoscopy when tolerable; do not force painful fissure examination
Deep pain without visible lesion → CT/MRI for occult abscess; recurrent fistula → pelvic MRI
Rectal bleeding with anemia, weight loss, bowel change, or screening indication → colon evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Fiber, fluids, stool softening, **sitz baths**; fissure → topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem
Refractory chronic fissure → botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy after continence-risk assessment
Internal hemorrhoids persisting despite conservative measures → rubber-band ligation; advanced prolapse → surgery
★ Abscess → **incision and drainage**; antibiotics added for cellulitis, systemic illness, or immunosuppression
Fistula → colorectal surgery; painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 72 hours → consider excision

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess recurrence, fistula, sepsis; sphincter injury → fecal incontinence
Chronic bleeding → iron deficiency; pruritus → excoriations and secondary infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting; gentle cleansing, dry skin, barrier ointment for seepage

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anal cancer: persistent irregular ulcer/mass, biopsy required
Proctitis: urgency, tenesmus, mucous discharge
Pinworm: nocturnal itch, especially children; tape test

table.title: Local patterns
rows: Tearing defecation pain; bright blood on paper
Recurrent purulent drainage from external opening

anorectal-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established colorectal teaching.

atheroembolic-disease.name: Atheroembolic disease
atheroembolic-disease.scope: Cholesterol crystal embolization, vascular procedures, livedo reticularis, blue toe syndrome, acute kidney injury, eosinophilia and hypocomplementemia, supportive management
atheroembolic-disease.core: Delayed kidney injury plus livedo reticularis or painful blue toes after arterial instrumentation suggests cholesterol crystal embolization.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Extensive aortic atherosclerosis, older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease
★ Recent **angiography, vascular surgery**, or aortic manipulation; occasionally spontaneous plaque disruption
Anticoagulation/thrombolysis may precipitate embolization but do not establish the diagnosis alone

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Intact distal pulses** despite digital ischemia; multifocal skin findings
Creatinine rises days to weeks after exposure rather than immediately
Eosinophilia, hypocomplementemia, elevated ESR; urinalysis often bland or mildly proteinuric/hematuric
Retinal cholesterol plaques, abdominal pain, GI bleeding, or neurologic deficits indicate additional organs involved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture releases cholesterol crystals into small arteries and arterioles
Mechanical occlusion plus foreign-body inflammation → progressive downstream tissue injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Characteristic clinical pattern often sufficient; review procedure timing and multisystem signs
Uncertain diagnosis → **skin biopsy** of accessible affected tissue; renal biopsy if needed
Histology: empty needle-shaped cholesterol clefts within occluded vessels; crystals dissolve during processing
Assess renal function, electrolytes, urinalysis; ultrasound excludes coincident obstructive renal injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive care**: manage BP, volume, electrolytes; dialysis for conventional urgent indications
High-intensity statin and vascular risk reduction; antiplatelet treatment for underlying atherosclerotic indications
Avoid further aortic instrumentation when possible; no routine thrombolysis or anticoagulation for crystal emboli
Continue anticoagulation only for compelling separate indications; routine corticosteroids lack established benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent kidney dysfunction, dialysis dependence, digital necrosis, bowel ischemia
Extensive systemic embolization → multiorgan failure and death

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lipid/BP/diabetes control; minimize unnecessary arterial procedures in severe aortic disease
Use less invasive vascular evaluation when sufficient; monitor renal function after high-risk interventions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contrast-associated AKI: onset within 24–72 hours, usually improves; no systemic embolic skin signs
Acute arterial thromboembolism: abrupt limb ischemia with diminished pulses
Vasculitis: inflammatory vessel injury, often active urine sediment; biopsy lacks cholesterol clefts

atheroembolic-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established cholesterol-embolization teaching.

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; lactation and milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: painless postlactational mass; fat–fluid level on imaging
Abscess: focal tender erythematous fluctuant mass, sometimes fever; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → papilloma or malignancy evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions
Adipose injury causes inflammatory necrosis and calcification that can resemble cancer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
Suspicious solid lesion or imaging–exam discordance → **core needle biopsy**
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior enhancement; no solid component
Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Simple painful cyst → aspiration; bloody fluid or residual mass → further tissue evaluation
Fibroadenoma → observe when concordant; excise if rapidly enlarging, large or symptomatic
Fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID; galactocele → aspiration if symptomatic
★ Abscess → ultrasound-guided drainage + **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**; MRSA risk → clindamycin
Continue breastfeeding/pumping with lactational infection; persistent pathologic discharge → breast surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent periductal abscess → fistula; incomplete drainage → persistent infection
Proliferative lesions with atypia increase future cancer risk; simple cysts do not

rows.label: Prevention
items: Effective breast emptying during lactation; smoking cessation for recurrent periductal disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cancer: irregular fixed mass, retraction or suspicious nodes
Phyllodes: rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass requiring excision

benign-breast-conditions.evidence: Not checked online; established breast diagnostic principles.

bladder-cancer.name: Bladder cancer
bladder-cancer.scope: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, painless gross hematuria, smoking and occupational exposures, cystoscopy, transurethral resection
bladder-cancer.core: Painless gross hematuria in an older adult requires evaluation for urinary tract malignancy, even during anticoagulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Smoking**, aromatic amines in dye/rubber industries; older age and male sex
Cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation; chronic catheter irritation and Schistosoma haematobium predispose to squamous carcinoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Intermittent bleeding, clots; carcinoma in situ may produce irritative voiding symptoms without a visible mass
Advanced disease: pelvic pain, hydronephrosis, weight loss, or bone pain

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Urothelial field injury → multifocal tumors and recurrence throughout the collecting system
Squamous metaplasia from chronic inflammation → keratinizing malignancy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Cystoscopy + CT urography** evaluate bladder and upper tracts; urinalysis/culture assess alternatives
Urine cytology helps detect high-grade disease/CIS; negative cytology does not exclude cancer
★ **TURBT including muscularis propria** establishes histology, grade, and depth
T1 disease → repeat resection within 6 weeks; invasive disease → chest/abdomen/pelvis staging

rows.label: Tx
items: Clot retention → large-bore catheter, irrigation; persistent obstruction or bleeding → urgent urology
Selected fit patients seeking bladder preservation → maximal resection plus concurrent chemoradiation
Avoid intravesical chemotherapy with suspected bladder perforation; BCG contraindicated during active symptomatic UTI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive renal failure, recurrent hemorrhage, nodal or distant metastases
Intravesical BCG → cystitis; rarely disseminated infection; cystectomy → diversion-related metabolic complications

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation and occupational protection; no routine population screening
★ **Surveillance cystoscopy** after treatment because recurrence is common; interval based on risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephrolithiasis: colicky flank pain, stone on noncontrast CT
Glomerulonephritis: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, proteinuria
Cystitis: dysuria and positive culture; persistent hematuria after treatment still needs evaluation

table.title: Depth determines definitive treatment
rows: TURBT + intravesical BCG; selected early cystectomy

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery, incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Partial obstruction may still permit stool or diarrhea; bowel movements do not exclude early obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal lesions → personality change; motor cortex → weakness; posterior fossa → ataxia
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Vestibular symptoms → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

burn-injuries.name: Burn injuries
burn-injuries.scope: Superficial, partial-thickness, full-thickness burns, total body surface area (Rule of Nines), fluid resuscitation (Parkland), smoke inhalation and airway edema, carbon monoxide/cyanide toxicity
burn-injuries.core: Burn severity depends on depth, affected surface area, location, and inhalation injury; airway threats and hypovolemia take priority over wound care.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Flames/scalds, electricity, chemicals; closed-space fires increase toxic inhalation risk
Older adults, children, impaired mobility/sensation; inconsistent injury history raises abuse concern

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hoarseness, stridor, oropharyngeal edema, soot** → threatened airway; skin burns may appear minor
CO: headache, confusion, syncope despite normal pulse oximetry
Cyanide: enclosed-fire exposure with cardiovascular collapse and severe lactic acidosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary leak → intravascular depletion and edema; swelling progresses after initial presentation
CO impairs oxygen transport; cyanide blocks mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TBSA excludes superficial burns**; adult Rule of Nines: head/each arm 9%, each leg 18%
Anterior/posterior trunk 18% each, perineum 1%; own palm including fingers ≈1%; children → Lund-Browder
★ Inhalation/toxin concern → **ABG with co-oximetry**, lactate; normal PaO2 does not exclude CO
Electrical burn → ECG, CK, urinalysis for rhabdomyolysis; small surface injury may hide deep damage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway threat → **intubate**; burn center: full-thickness, ≥10% partial, critical-site, inhalation/electrical/chemical
CO → 100% oxygen; severe neurologic/cardiac toxicity or pregnancy → consider hyperbaric oxygen; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin
Lactated Ringer: classic **Parkland = 4 mL × kg × %TBSA** during first 24 hours
Half by 8 hours from injury, remainder over 16; ABA now starts adults at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA

rows.label: Complications
items: Shock, AKI, infection, contractures, compartment syndrome; overresuscitation worsens edema
Restrictive chest/limb eschar → escharotomy; true compartment syndrome → fasciotomy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Titrate fluids to urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults; formula only starting estimate
Analgesia, cleaning, moist nonadherent dressings, tetanus; avoid routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis
★ **Stop exposure, remove jewelry, cool water**, prevent hypothermia; no ice
Smoke/CO detectors, safe water temperature, fire escape plan; early rehabilitation and range of motion

rows.label: Mimics
items: SJS/TEN: medication exposure, mucosal erosions, widespread epidermal detachment
Cellulitis: spreading warmth/erythema without immediate thermal exposure

table.title: Depth
rows: Moist blisters, brisk blanching, very painful

burn-injuries.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ABA burn resuscitation guideline 2024](https://academic.oup.com/jbcr/article/45/3/565/7458089); classic Parkland contrasted with current initial estimate.

colorectal-carcinoma.name: Colorectal carcinoma
colorectal-carcinoma.scope: Colon adenocarcinoma, rectal cancer, staging, surgical resection (hemicolectomy), liver metastases, chemotherapy
colorectal-carcinoma.core: Occult blood loss, altered bowel habits, or obstruction warrants colon evaluation; cancer stage determines local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, adenomas, Lynch/FAP, longstanding colitis, family history; smoking, obesity, processed meat

rows.label: Clues
items: Right-sided lesions → iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, occult bleeding
Left-sided lesions → constipation, narrowed stools, obstruction; rectal lesions → tenesmus/hematochezia
Weight loss, palpable mass; hepatomegaly or elevated ALP suggests hepatic spread

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adenoma–carcinoma sequence involves APC, KRAS, p53; mismatch-repair failure drives microsatellite instability
Portal drainage favors liver metastases; distal rectal tumors may spread directly to lungs

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with biopsy**; evaluate entire colon for synchronous tumors
★ Confirmed cancer → **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**, baseline CEA, tumor mismatch-repair/MSI testing
Rectal cancer → pelvic MRI for local staging; CEA cannot diagnose or screen
Obstruction/perforation → urgent contrast CT and surgical assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable colon cancer → **segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy**
Stage III → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX; selected high-risk stage II → individualized chemotherapy
Locally advanced rectal cancer → neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy/chemoradiation, then total mesorectal excision
MSI-high advanced disease → checkpoint inhibitor; selected liver metastases → resection after multidisciplinary assessment
Perforation or unstable obstruction → urgent operation; selected stable obstruction → stent or diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Bleeding, perforation, malignant obstruction; venous thrombosis; oxaliplatin neuropathy
Postoperative anastomotic leak; pelvic treatment → urinary/sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Average-risk screening **45–75 years**; earlier colonoscopy for strong family history/hereditary syndromes
Postresection colonoscopy, CEA and stage-based CT surveillance; remove premalignant polyps

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemorrhoids: outlet bleeding without explanatory anemia; do not dismiss alarm features
IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea; diverticulitis: acute focal pain and fever

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts increase pulmonary flow; longstanding vascular remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell → knee–chest position, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; irreversible Eisenmenger physiology → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

corneal-abrasion.name: Corneal abrasion
corneal-abrasion.scope: Corneal abrasion, corneal foreign body, fluorescein examination, topical antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, chemical eye injury
corneal-abrasion.core: Acute painful red eye after surface trauma; exclude an open globe, retained foreign body, and infectious keratitis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fingernail or plant injury, airborne debris, contact lenses, eye rubbing
High-velocity metalwork suggests intraocular foreign body; alkali exposure penetrates deeply

rows.label: Clues
items: Foreign-body sensation, tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm; vision usually preserved unless central involvement
★ Reduced visual acuity, irregular pupil, hyphema, severe mechanism → urgent ophthalmology
Vertical linear scratches suggest retained material beneath upper eyelid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epithelial loss exposes densely innervated cornea; superficial defects generally heal within 24–48 hours
Chemical injury damages epithelium; severe alkali exposure causes stromal and limbal ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Visual acuity → slit-lamp/**fluorescein** examination; evert upper lid for retained particles
Positive Seidel sign: aqueous streaming through fluorescein → open globe; avoid tonometry or manipulation
Suspected intraocular foreign body → orbital CT; avoid MRI if metal possible
Persistent pain beyond expected healing → reassess for ulcer, foreign body, or recurrent erosion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Chemical exposure → immediate copious irrigation; remove particles, continue until stable physiologic pH
Loose surface foreign body → saline irrigation/moistened swab; embedded object or rust ring → trained removal
★ Uncomplicated abrasion → topical **erythromycin**; contact lens-related → ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin for Pseudomonas
Oral NSAID/acetaminophen; no pressure patching or routine take-home topical anesthetic; avoid topical steroids
Open globe → rigid shield, NPO, IV antibiotics, emergency ophthalmology; never remove protruding object

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacterial keratitis, corneal ulcer, scarring, recurrent corneal erosion
Chemical burns: limbal stem-cell loss, corneal melting, glaucoma, permanent visual impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Eye protection; stop contacts until healed; replace contaminated lenses and case
Tetanus prophylaxis: penetrating/contaminated wounds by vaccine history; unnecessary for clean superficial abrasion
Contact lens injury, large/central defect, persistent symptoms → review within 24 hours

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV keratitis: dendritic fluorescein pattern with terminal bulbs
Corneal ulcer: white stromal infiltrate with epithelial defect
Acute angle closure: fixed mid-dilated pupil, markedly elevated IOP

diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or selected TCAs alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Radiculopathy: dermatomal unilateral pain with root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid enlargement, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Low bone density, infertility, cardiac failure; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.name: Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.scope: Esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula types, VACTERL association, coiled nasogastric tube on chest x-ray
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.core: A newborn with excessive oral secretions, choking and cyanosis during feeds requires evaluation for esophageal atresia or tracheoesophageal fistula.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prenatal polyhydramnios and small/absent stomach bubble suggest impaired fetal swallowing
Associated anomalies: **VACTERL**—vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb defects

rows.label: Clues
items: Frothy drooling, feeding-associated respiratory distress, recurrent desaturation or aspiration
★ **Nasogastric/orogastric tube cannot pass** into stomach; avoid repeated forceful attempts
Abdominal distention suggests airway-to-stomach communication; isolated atresia often has gasless abdomen
H-type fistula: esophagus patent, delayed recurrent pneumonia or cough with liquids

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal foregut separation leaves esophageal discontinuity and/or connection to trachea
Secretions pool proximally; distal communication permits reflux aspiration and gastric inflation during ventilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Gentle radiopaque tube placement → **chest/abdominal radiograph showing proximal coiling**
Distal bowel gas supports distal fistula; absent gas favors no distal connection
Routine contrast feeding unnecessary in classic atresia; aspiration can worsen lung injury
Suspected H-type → carefully supervised contrast esophagram and bronchoscopy
Echocardiography before surgery; assess anus, kidneys, spine and limbs for associated anomalies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, head elevation, continuous proximal pouch suction**, IV fluids and pediatric surgical referral
Secure airway if respiratory failure; minimize bag-mask ventilation because fistula can inflate stomach
★ Definitive → **fistula ligation and esophageal anastomosis** after stabilization
Long-gap atresia → staged nutritional and reconstructive plan; aspiration pneumonia → IV antibiotics
Feeding resumed after postoperative assessment of repair integrity and swallowing safety

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, anastomotic leak/stricture, recurrent fistula, reflux and dysmotility
Associated tracheomalacia can cause persistent noisy breathing, cyanotic spells or recurrent respiratory infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prenatal recognition enables delivery planning; aspiration precautions until repaired
Long-term monitoring for dysphagia, reflux, growth failure and recurrent respiratory symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choanal atresia: cyanosis improves with crying; nasal catheter obstructed
Laryngeal cleft: aspiration with patent esophagus
Pyloric stenosis: later nonbilious vomiting without tube coiling

fat-embolism-syndrome.name: Fat embolism syndrome
fat-embolism-syndrome.scope: Long-bone fractures, triade of hypoxemia, neurologic impairment, petechial rash, supportive management
fat-embolism-syndrome.core: Respiratory failure, altered mental status, and petechiae appearing 24–72 hours after major skeletal trauma suggest systemic fat embolization.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Femoral/tibial or pelvic fractures, multiple fractures, intramedullary instrumentation
Occasionally major burns, pancreatitis or liposuction; young adults with high-energy trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypoxemia preceding neurologic deterioration** after an initially stable interval
Nondependent petechiae over upper chest, axillae, conjunctivae; rash may be transient or absent
Tachypnea, fever, tachycardia; confusion, agitation, seizures or coma
Thrombocytopenia, falling hemoglobin; retinal hemorrhages or cotton-wool lesions

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow fat enters venules → pulmonary microvascular obstruction; free fatty acids trigger endothelial injury
Systemic passage through shunts/capillaries → cerebral, retinal and skin injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; no single definitive laboratory test
ABG assesses oxygenation; chest radiograph → diffuse bilateral infiltrates rather than focal consolidation
CT pulmonary angiography may exclude thrombotic PE but miss microvascular fat emboli
Cerebral symptoms with nondiagnostic head CT → MRI diffusion **starfield pattern** supports diagnosis
Fat globules in urine/sputum nonspecific; not required for diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen and supportive critical care**; intubation with lung-protective ventilation for respiratory failure
Maintain perfusion with careful IV fluids; treat shock and associated traumatic injuries
Stabilize fractures after resuscitation; avoid unnecessary manipulation
Heparin and glucocorticoids not established treatments for manifest syndrome

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, right ventricular strain, persistent neurologic injury or death
Ventilator-associated complications; most survivors recover with supportive treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Early immobilization and timely fixation of long-bone fractures after stabilization
VTE prophylaxis prevents concurrent thrombotic disease, not the fat-embolism mechanism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Thrombotic PE: larger-vessel filling defect, usually no petechial/neurologic combination
Pulmonary contusion: immediate post-trauma focal injury; aspiration: witnessed event or dependent infiltrates

rows: At injury; evolves over first day

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation; cholecystectomy → bile-duct injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gastrointestinal-perforation.name: Gastrointestinal perforation
gastrointestinal-perforation.scope: Gastroduodenal perforation, bowel perforation (diverticular, appendiceal, iatrogenic), pneumoperitoneum (subdiaphragmatic free air), acute peritonitis, IV antibiotics, emergent exploratory laparotomy
gastrointestinal-perforation.core: Abrupt severe abdominal pain with guarding, rigidity, and free intraperitoneal air suggests a perforated viscus requiring rapid resuscitation and source control.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Peptic ulcer disease, NSAIDs, H. pylori; diverticulitis, appendicitis, obstruction, ischemia, malignancy
Recent endoscopy/surgery, penetrating/blunt trauma; glucocorticoids/immunosuppression can blunt peritoneal findings

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, tachycardia, absent bowel sounds, distension; pain with movement/cough
★ **Hypotension, confusion, oliguria, elevated lactate** → septic shock/organ hypoperfusion
Retroperitoneal or contained leaks may lack diffuse rigidity or visible free air

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal contents spill into peritoneum → chemical inflammation followed by bacterial infection and sepsis
Fluid sequestration and vasodilation reduce effective circulating volume

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable patient → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** to localize leak and abscess
Upright chest radiograph: subdiaphragmatic free air; negative film does not exclude perforation
CBC, metabolic panel, lactate, blood cultures if septic, type/crossmatch; pregnancy test when relevant
★ **Unstable with generalized peritonitis → surgery**, without delaying for CT
Avoid barium studies or diagnostic endoscopy when perforation suspected; water-soluble contrast only for selected questions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, large-bore IVs, isotonic crystalloid**, analgesia; immediate surgical consultation
★ Prompt **piperacillin-tazobactam** or ceftriaxone + metronidazole; cover enteric gram-negatives/anaerobes
Nasogastric decompression for upper GI leak/ileus; IV proton-pump inhibitor for ulcer perforation
Urgent operative repair/resection and washout for free perforation; norepinephrine if shock persists after fluids
Selected stable contained leak may receive antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage with close surgical observation

rows.label: Complications
items: Intra-abdominal abscess, septic shock, multiorgan failure, fistula; anastomotic leak after repair

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H. pylori after ulcer disease; avoid unnecessary NSAIDs, use gastroprotection when ulcer risk high
Treat causal disease, optimize postoperative leak recognition; reassess persistent fever/pain after procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pancreatitis: elevated lipase, characteristic epigastric/back pain without typical pneumoperitoneum
Mesenteric ischemia: initially pain out of proportion; later peritonitis indicates necrosis/perforation
Postoperative free air: may be expected, but instability/peritonitis demands leak evaluation

hip-fractures.name: Hip fractures
hip-fractures.scope: Femoral neck fracture, intertrochanteric fracture, avascular necrosis, preoperative stabilization, surgical repair
hip-fractures.core: An older adult unable to bear weight after a fall may have a hip fracture even when initial radiographs are normal.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Osteoporosis, frailty, prior fragility fracture, impaired vision/balance, sedatives
Young adults: high-energy trauma; consider pathologic fracture when mechanism is minimal and imaging atypical

rows.label: Clues
items: Groin/hip pain, pain with passive rotation or axial loading
★ Displaced injury: **shortened, externally rotated leg**; impacted fractures may allow some walking
Assess distal perfusion, neurologic function, other trauma; document preinjury mobility and cognition

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intracapsular displacement can disrupt retinacular branches of medial circumflex femoral artery
Extracapsular region has better blood supply but can bleed substantially into surrounding tissues

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP pelvis + lateral hip radiographs**; avoid forceful frog-leg positioning in suspected fracture
★ Persistent suspicion with negative x-ray → **MRI**; CT if MRI unavailable/contraindicated
CBC, electrolytes, renal function, ECG, type/screen; assess anticoagulant use and reversible medical instability

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, consider fascia iliaca block; IV fluids for depletion, pressure protection
★ **Repair within 24–48 hours** after correcting major instability; avoid unnecessary testing delays
Reverse relevant anticoagulation for surgery; perioperative antibiotics and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis when safe
Early weight bearing/mobilization, PT/OT, delirium prevention; orthogeriatric co-management improves recovery
Nonoperative care reserved for selected palliative situations after goals-of-care discussion

rows.label: Complications
items: Femoral neck: avascular necrosis, nonunion; intertrochanteric: blood loss
VTE, delirium, pneumonia, pressure injury, loss of independence, increased mortality
Arthroplasty: dislocation/infection; monitor postoperative neurovascular status and wound

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Fragility fracture → **osteoporosis treatment**, adequate calcium/vitamin D, fall-risk reduction
Medication review, balance/strength training, home safety and assistive device assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hip dislocation: high-energy trauma, abnormal fixed rotation; urgent reduction
Greater trochanteric pain: lateral tenderness, generally preserved weight bearing
Pelvic insufficiency fracture: sacral/pelvic pain, may require MRI
